summary: Estonia is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period (with ETIAS being phased in), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa. Russian citizens face additional entry restrictions even with a valid Schengen visa.

The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia — visa information

fee.notes: For work, study, family and other stays over 90 days; can be issued for up to a year. Confirm the current fee and requirements with the Estonian mission.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia — visa information

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia — visa information

proofOfFunds.text: Estonian law ties the required means of subsistence to the national minimum wage (0.2 times the monthly minimum wage per day of stay); in practice officers assess sufficiency case by case alongside accommodation and tickets. Confirm the current figure with the Estonian mission.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia — visa information

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Estonia is one of Europe’s most digital societies. Cards and contactless payments work everywhere, from market stalls to rural cafés, and you can comfortably visit without handling cash.

safety.text: Estonia is a very safe destination with low crime. Take normal precautions against pickpocketing in Tallinn’s Old Town in high season, and take care on icy pavements in winter.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Estonia Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September brings long white nights, island trips and café terraces; December is worth the cold for Tallinn’s Christmas market, one of Europe’s prettiest.

idp.text: Estonia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Estonia yet.

tips.text: Do not plan to enter or leave via the Estonia–Russia land border: crossings are heavily restricted, and Russian citizens with Schengen visas issued for tourism are refused entry to Estonia — only narrow exemptions apply.

Non-EU visitors are registered biometrically in the EU Entry/Exit System at the border, and the ETIAS travel authorization is being phased in for visa-exempt travelers. Check the official EU site before you fly.
Leave the cash at home — Estonia is nearly fully cashless, and cards or phones are accepted everywhere including buses, markets and tiny island shops.
From November to March expect short daylight hours, sub-zero temperatures and icy pavements — pack proper footwear and warm layers, and check ferry schedules to the islands in advance.
Estonia combines easily with Latvia and Lithuania by bus or with Helsinki by a 2-hour ferry. All are Schengen, so your 90/180-day allowance is shared, not reset, when you cross.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Estonia?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (€90) from an Estonian mission or a Schengen state representing Estonia.

faq.question: Does time in Estonia count against my Schengen 90-day limit?
faq.answer: Yes. Estonia is fully in the Schengen Area, so days spent there count toward the single 90-days-in-180 allowance shared with all other Schengen countries.

faq.question: Can Russian citizens enter Estonia with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Generally no. Estonia bars Russian citizens holding Schengen visas issued for tourism from entering, and land-border crossings from Russia are heavily restricted. Only narrow exemptions apply, such as residents, family members of EU citizens and humanitarian cases. Check with the Estonian authorities before traveling.

faq.question: Do I need ETIAS to visit Estonia?
faq.answer: Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, visa-exempt non-EU travelers will need the €20 online authorization before traveling to Estonia and the rest of the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU ETIAS site for the current status.

faq.question: Can I visit Helsinki from Tallinn without extra formalities?
faq.answer: Yes. The Tallinn–Helsinki ferry is a domestic-style Schengen crossing with no routine passport control, though you should always carry your passport or ID. Days in Finland draw on the same Schengen 90/180 allowance.
